title: Spark Savings ETH pays depositors the liquidity layer's yield explicitly net of the idle redemption buffer
content:
A.6.1.1.1.3.5.3.2.3.3 gives the ETH vault a formula rather than a benchmark: the Rewards Rate equals "the supply-weighted average yield of ETH-denominated assets held in the Spark Liquidity Layer, **multiplied by one minus the percentage of spETH backing held in the spETH vault contract for instant redemptions**, plus the Spark Savings ETH Spread" — the spread itself "defined as part of the ALM Planner configuration process," bounded to a range of −0.5% to 2%.

The middle factor is the interesting one. Assets sitting in the vault for instant redemption earn nothing; only the deployed remainder earns the liquidity layer's yield. Multiplying by (1 − buffer share) passes that dilution straight through to depositors, so the advertised rate is arithmetically what the pool actually earns.

The alternative — quoting the gross deployed yield and absorbing the buffer's cost from elsewhere — would mean Spark subsidizing liquidity out of its own margin, and would create a perverse incentive to shrink the buffer to protect the headline rate. Here the cost of liquidity is borne by the people who benefit from it, and Spark has no rate-driven reason to under-provision.

The bounded spread does the remaining work. It is Spark's margin, and permitting it to go **negative** to −0.5% is a deliberate allowance to pay depositors *more* than the pool earns — a subsidy lever for bootstrapping a new vault, capped tightly enough that it cannot become a structural loss.

This is the most transparent rate definition in the Spark Artifact: a reader with chain data can compute what the vault should be paying, and any divergence is a fact about the setter's performance rather than an ambiguity in the policy.
description: The rate equals the supply-weighted ETH yield times one minus the share of spETH backing held for instant redemptions, plus a spread bounded between −0.5% and 2%.
